title: The Broken Code Machine
covers: how the commutative, associative and identity properties rewrite an expression without changing its value, and why subtraction and division cannot be swapped or regrouped
cert: rewriting expressions with the commutative, associative and identity properties

intro.caption: Lesson 6-8 — using properties to write equivalent expressions. Ozzie built a machine that scrambles secret codes. It is supposed to change how a code LOOKS, never what it is WORTH. Three reader gates and a boss repair stand between the cadets and a working machine.

balloons.t: Meet the Shuffler. It scrambles codes. The value stays the same.
In theory. Today it ate three messages.
Easy fix. Order never matters. 9 − 4 or 4 − 9, same thing. That's classified.
Not classified. Just wrong. 9 − 4 is 5. But 4 − 9 is not 5.

pages.caption: The Shuffler has a swap gear. It changes the ORDER of numbers. Some swaps keep the value. Some swaps break the message.

balloons.t: Gear one swaps the order. Which swaps are safe?
Clue: the broken ones had − or ÷.
Gear two moves the parentheses. The numbers stay in the same order.
Same numbers. New grouping. Does the value change? Check.
Last gear. It adds 0 or multiplies by 1. The value stays exactly the same.
A gear that changes nothing? Finally, a gear like me.
My squad's machine never jams. Yours swaps minus signs. Cute.
Watch us fix it. One gear at a time.

win.caption: Commutative: change the order. Associative: change the grouping. Identity: add 0 or multiply by 1. Commutative and associative work for addition and multiplication, but NOT for subtraction or division.

gates.title: Gate 1 · The Swap Gear
gates.prompt: The swap gear changes the order of numbers. Name the property, then test which swaps are safe.
hints: Conceptual: a swap is safe only if both sides have the same value. Work out each side and compare.
Procedural: compute the left side, then the right side. Equal values mean the swap is safe.

steps: Practice: the gear turns 2 × 9 into 9 × 2. Both are 18, so the value stays. That is the Commutative Property.
Now test 9 − 2 and 2 − 9. 9 − 2 = 7, but taking 9 away from 2 does not give 7.
So addition and multiplication can swap. Subtraction cannot.

items.q: The gear turns 6 + 9 into 9 + 6. Which property is this?

options.fb: Associative moves the parentheses. Here there are no parentheses. Only the order changed.
Identity means adding 0 or multiplying by 1. There is no 0 or 1 here.
Distributive multiplies a number by everything in parentheses. Nothing is multiplied here.

items.q: Which swaps keep the same value? Select all that apply.

options.fb: Both sides are 21. Multiplication can swap.
10 − 4 = 6, but 4 − 10 is not 6. Subtraction is NOT commutative.
Both sides are 17. Addition can swap.
8 ÷ 2 = 4, but 2 ÷ 8 = ¼. Division is NOT commutative.

items.fbMiss: One more swap is safe. Compute both sides of every swap.
items.fbExtra: One of those swaps changes the value. Compute both sides.

gates.pass: The swap gear now locks on minus and divide. 9 − 4 stays 9 − 4. Teo says he knew that all along.

gates.title: Gate 2 · The Bracket Gear
gates.prompt: The bracket gear moves the parentheses. The numbers stay in the same order.
hints: Conceptual: parentheses say what to do first. Moving them changes the grouping, not the order.
Procedural: pick a grouping that makes an easy number, like 10 or 100. Then work out both groupings and compare.

steps: Group 9 + 1 first: it makes 10. Then 6 + 10 = 16. The other way: 15 + 1 = 16.
Same numbers, same order, new grouping, same value. That is the Associative Property.

items.q: The gear turns (8 + 7) + 3 into 8 + (7 + 3). Which property is this?

options.fb: The order stayed 8, 7, 3. Only the parentheses moved, so it is not a swap.
Nothing adds 0 or multiplies by 1 here.
No number multiplies a sum here. It is all addition.

fb.msg: 85 is only 17 × 5. You still need to multiply by 2.
24 is 17 + 5 + 2. These are times signs, not plus signs.

items.fbDefault: Group 5 × 2 first. It makes 10. Then multiply 17 by 10.

items.q: Teo runs the bracket gear on subtraction: (12 − 5) − 3 and 12 − (5 − 3). Same value?

options.fb: 12 − (5 − 3) = 12 − 2 = 10, not 4. Regrouping subtraction changes the value.

options.t: No: one is 4, the other is 10

options.fb: (12 − 5) − 3 = 7 − 3 = 4, not 10. Do the parentheses first.

options.t: No: one is 4, the other is 14
options.fb: 5 − 3 = 2, and 12 − 2 = 10, not 14. Subtract inside the parentheses first.

gates.pass: The bracket gear clicks in. It regroups plus and times, and it leaves minus alone. 17 × 10 = 170.

gates.title: Gate 3 · The Do-Nothing Gear
gates.prompt: The tiny gear adds 0 or multiplies by 1. Find the number that changes nothing.
hints: Conceptual: adding 0 keeps a number the same. Multiplying by 1 keeps a number the same.
Procedural: try your number in the blank. Does the left side come out equal to the right side?

steps: Practice: m + 0 = m. Adding 0 does not change m.
Careful: 8 × 0 = 0. Multiplying by 0 is NOT the identity.

options.fb: Multiplying by 0 makes 0, not y. The identity for multiplying is 1.
That swaps the order. It is the Commutative Property.
That moves the parentheses. It is the Associative Property.

items.aria: number added to 37 that keeps it 37

fb.msg: 37 + 1 = 38. Adding 1 changes the value. What can you add that changes nothing?

items.fbDefault: Which number can you add without changing anything?

items.aria: number multiplied by 54 that keeps it 54

fb.msg: 54 × 0 = 0, not 54. For multiplying, the number that changes nothing is not 0.

items.fbDefault: How many groups of 54 make exactly 54?

gates.pass: The tiny gear spins. Plus 0, times 1, and every code keeps its value. Chip calls it the Teo gear.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Repair the Machine
gates.prompt: Fix the broken setting first. Then run the whole machine: put its moves in order and name the gears.
hints: Conceptual: each line of the machine changes only one thing: the order, the grouping, or a 0 or 1.
Procedural: compare two lines. If only the order changed, it is commutative. If only the parentheses moved, it is associative.

steps: Swap 8 and 5: 5 + (5 + 8). Commutative. Move the parentheses: (5 + 5) + 8. Associative.

items.q: The machine turned 20 − 8 into 8 − 20, and 20 ÷ 4 into 4 ÷ 20. What is the repair?

options.fb: 20 − 8 = 12, but 8 − 20 is not 12. That is Teo's mistake.

options.t: Lock the swap gear on + and ×
options.fb: Swaps on + and × are safe: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3 and 3 × 5 = 5 × 3. Those are not the problem.
Adding 0 keeps a value the same, but it does not undo a swapped subtraction.

options.t: Lock the swap and bracket gears on − and ÷

items.q: Tap the machine's lines in order, from 4 + (9 + 6) to 10 + 9.
items.fb: Start at 4 + (9 + 6). Swap 9 and 6 first. Then move the parentheses so 4 + 6 sits together. Then add.

items.q: Which gears did the machine use, in order, to get from line 1 to line 3?

options.fb: Line 1 to line 2 only swapped 9 and 6. That is a swap, so it comes first.
No line adds 0 or multiplies by 1, so the identity gear never ran.
Line 2 to line 3 keeps the order 4, 6, 9. Only the parentheses moved.

gates.pass: WHIRR. Every message comes out scrambled but worth exactly the same. Vale checks it twice and finds nothing.

journal.heading: Lesson 6-8 — what the code machine taught us
rows: Change the order, keep the value: 6 + 9 = 9 + 6 and 7 × 3 = 3 × 7.
Change the grouping, keep the value: (8 + 7) + 3 = 8 + (7 + 3). Group to make 10: 17 × (5 × 2) = 170.
Adding 0 or multiplying by 1 changes nothing: 37 + 0 = 37 and 54 × 1 = 54.
Every line the machine writes is worth the same. 4 + (9 + 6) and 10 + 9 are both 19.
Subtraction and division do NOT swap or regroup: 10 − 4 = 6, but 4 − 10 is not 6.
journal.quote: "Swap a minus sign and the message breaks. Swap Teo's opinion and nothing changes." — Chip

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 6-8 (Generate Equivalent Expressions) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: the commutative, associative and identity properties of addition and multiplication, writing equivalent expressions, and why subtraction and division do not commute or regroup.
standards: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions
